subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Conspicuous Consumption
description: A short lesson to help you apply Conspicuous Consumption.

hook.text: A $300 white T-shirt with a luxury logo outsells a $10 identical one. The fabric is the same. The signal is not.

buildup.text: Veblen coined conspicuous consumption in 1899: people buy expensive goods to signal wealth and social status.

discovery.text: The value is not in the product. It is in the audience. Luxury goods are performances of status for others to observe.

twist.text: Quiet luxury reverses the signal. Ultra-wealthy hide logos because showing wealth has become the middle-class signal.

climax.text: Every purchase carries a social signal. Recognizing this separates what you want from what you want others to see.

punchline.text: You are not buying the thing. You are buying the signal.

quiz.question: What is conspicuous consumption?
options: Buying expensive goods to signal social status
Consuming goods in excess due to scarcity fears

details.summary: Conspicuous consumption is spending on visible luxury goods to signal wealth and social status. Thorstein Veblen identified this pattern in 1899, showing that some goods are valued precisely because they are expensive and visible to others.
details.whyItMatters: Conspicuous consumption represents trillions in global spending driven by social signaling rather than utility. Understanding it explains why luxury brands thrive during inequality and why status goods resist normal demand curves.
takeaways: Expensive goods signal wealth and status to social observers
Demand for some goods increases as price rises because higher cost signals more
Conspicuous consumption rises with economic inequality

faq.question: Why would demand increase when price increases?
faq.answer: For Veblen goods, the high price is the point. A $500 handbag that drops to $50 loses its signaling value. The expensive price tag communicates that the owner can afford to waste money, which is the signal that creates social value.

faq.question: Is conspicuous consumption only about rich people?
faq.answer: No. Research shows that lower-income individuals often spend a larger proportion of their income on visible status goods like branded clothing and cars. When other signals of status are unavailable, visible consumption becomes more important.
